items.prose: Use the round figures of this level.
items.question: Order these from fastest to slowest.

lines.text: A round trip inside one data centre

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall each round figure, then sort them.

byKey.dc: A round trip in one data centre is 500 µs: slower than NVMe, faster than a seek.
byKey.nvme: An NVMe read is 100 µs, five times faster than a data-centre round trip.

explain.text: Register 0.3 ns, L2 4 ns, DRAM 100 ns and NVMe 100 µs. Then a data-centre round trip at 500 µs and a disk seek at 10 ms. The network inside a building still beats a spinning disk.

items.prose: A handler has a 5 µs budget per message. It makes one main-memory read.
items.question: What percentage of the budget does that read use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 100 ns by 5,000 ns.

byKey.l1: 0.02% is an L1 read of 1 ns.
byKey.tenth: 20% would be 1,000 ns. A main-memory read is 100 ns.

explain.text: $100 / 5{,}000 = 0.02$, which is 2%. Fifty such reads would use the whole budget.

items.prose: A loop reads every third double of a 96-double array. The cache is cold and large, with 64-byte lines.
items.question: How many reads miss?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lines the reads touch.

byKey.each: Not every read misses: some share a line with the read before.
byKey.third: A stride of 3 is shorter than a line, so it touches every line.

explain.text: 96 doubles fill 12 lines. A stride of 3 is under 8, so every line is touched once: 12 misses in 32 reads.

items.prose: A 1,000 × 1,000 matrix of doubles is stored row by row: 8 MB, far bigger than the caches.
items.question: Which loop nest sums it fastest?

options.text: Row index outer, column index inner
Column index outer, row index inner
options.why: That jumps 8,000 bytes per read, so every read misses.

options.text: Either: the cache makes them equal
options.why: Only when the matrix fits in the cache. 8 MB does not.

feedback.correct: Row outer: the inner loop walks memory in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which order reads neighbours in memory?

explain.text: Row by row, each 64-byte line serves 8 reads. Column by column, each read lands on a new line. The inner loop should walk the contiguous index.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split 10,812 into page and offset.

byKey.frame: 49,152 is the start of frame 12. Add the offset 2,620.
byKey.same: The address must go through the table.
byKey.frame2: Frame 3 belongs to page 1. 10,812 is in page 2.

explain.text: $10{,}812 = 2 \times 4{,}096 + 2{,}620$: page 2, offset 2,620. Frame 12 gives $49{,}152 + 2{,}620 = 51{,}772$. In hex the offset 0xA3C survives untouched.

items.prose: A program first touches 2 GiB with 4 KiB pages. Each minor fault costs about 1 µs.
items.question: How many ms do the faults take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pages first.

byKey.pages: 524,288 is the number of faults. Each takes 1 µs.

explain.text: $2^{31} / 2^{12} = 524{,}288$ pages, and 524,288 µs is 524.288 ms. Touching the memory at start-up keeps that out of the session.

items.prose: `struct { uint8_t a; uint16_t b; uint8_t c; uint32_t d; uint8_t e; }` is 16 bytes as declared.
items.question: What is its size with the fields sorted largest first?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lay out `d`, `b`, then the three single bytes.

byKey.sum: 9 is where the data ends. Round up to the 4-byte alignment.

explain.text: `d` at 0, `b` at 4, then `a`, `c`, `e` at 6, 7 and 8. The data ends at 9, which rounds up to 12.

items.prose: A two-bit counter starts at 1. It guesses taken at 2 or 3, and moves up on T and down on N.
items.question: How many wrong guesses on `TTTN` repeated four times?

widget.accept: 5: the first T and the four N.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the counter through the first loop.

byKey.four: Count the first T too: at c = 1 the guess is N.
byKey.onebit: 8 is a one-bit predictor's count, wrong twice per loop exit.

explain.text: The first T is wrong, then each N is wrong once. One N only drops the counter from 3 to 2, so the next T is right. That is 1 + 4 = 5.

items.prose: An array of 24-byte structs starts on a 64-byte line boundary.
items.question: How many of the first 8 structs cross a line boundary?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each struct's first and last byte.

byKey.none: 64 is not a multiple of 24, so some must cross.
byKey.three: Struct 7 runs from byte 168 to 191, inside one line.

explain.text: Struct 2 runs from byte 48 to 71 and struct 5 from 120 to 143; both cross. The 8 structs fill 192 bytes, exactly 3 lines, so the pattern repeats. A 32-byte struct never crosses.
